narration: In the deep sea, at least nine of every ten species have no name.
The deep ocean hosts an estimated one million species, though fewer than ten percent have been formally described.
That figure comes from Ocean Census, and it is a model, not a count.
Researchers extrapolate from sampling effort, habitat area, and how often new species turn up on each expedition.
Published estimates of the described share range from five to fifteen percent.
The evidence shows that the deep is inhabited all the way into its trenches.
It does not tell us how many species are there, or how most of them live.
What lives in the depths of the ocean?
The deep sea is generally defined as the ocean below two hundred meters, where sunlight no longer supports photosynthesis.
This boundary is called the aphotic zone. Below it, organisms cannot rely on primary production from plants or algae.
They depend instead on organic matter falling from the surface, on chemosynthesis at hydrothermal vents and cold seeps, or on each other.

NOAA Ocean Exploration states that the deep ocean comprises roughly ninety-five percent of the ocean's volume and more than sixty percent of Earth's surface lies beneath waters deeper than two hundred meters.
The aphotic zone is subdivided. The bathyal zone extends from two hundred to four thousand meters.
The abyssal zone spans four thousand to six thousand meters. The hadal zone includes all trenches deeper than six thousand meters.
Each zone has distinct pressure, temperature, and biological communities. Pressure increases by approximately one atmosphere for every ten meters of depth.
At four thousand meters, pressure is roughly four hundred times surface pressure.
At eleven thousand meters in the Mariana Trench, it exceeds one thousand atmospheres.

Most deep-sea animals produce light. Estimates suggest that seventy-six percent of pelagic animals in the mesopelagic and bathypelagic zones are bioluminescent, according to research summarized by MBARI.
They generate light through chemical reactions, typically involving the enzyme luciferase and the substrate luciferin.

The light serves multiple functions: attracting prey, confusing predators, communicating with mates, and camouflaging the animal's silhouette against downwelling light from above, a strategy called counterillumination.
The anglerfish uses a bioluminescent lure extending from its head to attract prey in complete darkness.
The light is produced by symbiotic bacteria housed in the lure. Only female anglerfish possess the lure.
Males are much smaller and, in some species, become parasitic, fusing to the female's body and relying on her bloodstream for nutrients.
This extreme sexual dimorphism is an adaptation to the difficulty of finding mates in a vast, dark environment.
In nineteen seventy-seven, scientists aboard the submersible Alvin discovered hydrothermal vents on the Galápagos Rift.
The vents were surrounded by dense communities of tube worms, clams, and mussels, thriving in complete darkness.

These organisms do not depend on photosynthesis. They rely on chemosynthetic bacteria that oxidize hydrogen sulfide and other chemicals in the vent fluid, converting chemical energy into organic compounds.
The bacteria live symbiotically inside the tissues of tube worms and other vent fauna.
This process, chemosynthesis, was first confirmed at these vents in nineteen seventy-seven, according to NOAA Ocean Exploration.
Giant tube worms, Riftia pachyptila, can exceed two meters in length. They have no mouth, no gut, and no anus.
They absorb hydrogen sulfide and oxygen through a specialized organ called a plume, and house chemosynthetic bacteria in an internal organ called a trophosome.

The bacteria provide all the worm's nutrition. Riftia can tolerate temperatures ranging from two degrees Celsius in ambient seawater to above sixty degrees near vent openings, according to research published by Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.

The hadal zone includes the ocean's deepest trenches. The Mariana Trench reaches a maximum surveyed depth of ten thousand nine hundred and ninety-four meters, measured by the Five Deeps Expedition in twenty nineteen.

At these depths, pressure exceeds one thousand atmospheres. Organisms must have specialized adaptations: flexible cell membranes, pressure-resistant proteins, and the absence of gas-filled spaces that would collapse.
The deepest fish ever recorded is a snailfish, Pseudoliparis swirei, filmed at eight thousand one hundred and seventy-eight meters in the Mariana Trench by an international team in twenty seventeen.
Amphipods, small crustaceans, have been recovered from ten thousand nine hundred and eighteen meters.
These animals feed on organic matter that sinks from above and on the carcasses of larger animals that fall to the trench floor.
Hadal trenches are not barren. They are hotspots of scavenging activity and microbial diversity.
The giant squid, Architeuthis dux, inhabits depths between three hundred and one thousand meters.
The largest confirmed specimen measured thirteen meters in total length. Giant squid are rarely observed alive.
Most knowledge comes from specimens washed ashore or recovered from the stomachs of sperm whales, which dive to over two thousand meters to hunt them.

The first video of a living giant squid in its natural habitat was captured in twenty twelve by a team from NOAA, the Discovery Channel, and Japan's National Museum of Nature and Science, at a depth of six hundred and thirty meters off Japan.
Sperm whales are the deepest-diving mammals. They can reach depths exceeding two thousand meters and hold their breath for over ninety minutes.
They use echolocation to hunt in complete darkness. Their primary prey includes squid, octopus, and deep-sea fish.
The whale's ability to withstand extreme pressure is due to a collapsible ribcage, reduced air spaces, and high concentrations of myoglobin in muscle tissue, which stores oxygen.
How do we know an animal behaves a certain way when we've seen it three times?
Deep-sea organisms are studied using remotely operated vehicles, autonomous underwater vehicles, trawls, baited cameras, and submersibles.
Each method has biases. Trawls damage fragile organisms. Cameras only record what swims or crawls into view.
ROVs are limited by battery life and tether length. Submersibles provide direct human observation but are expensive and rare.
Most deep-sea species have been seen fewer than ten times. Behavior, reproduction, and lifespan are often inferred from anatomy, gut contents, and analogy to shallow-water relatives.
The estimate that fewer than ten percent of deep-sea species have been described comes from the gap between predicted diversity and the number of named species.
The Census of Marine Life, a decade-long international effort completed in twenty ten, added thousands of new species but concluded that the majority of marine life remains undiscovered.
The prediction of one million deep-sea species is based on models that extrapolate from sampling effort, habitat area, and the rate of new species discovery per unit effort.
The percentage is an estimate, not a census result. Published estimates of the described fraction range from five to fifteen percent, with ten percent commonly cited as a midpoint.
Microbial life in the deep ocean and beneath the seafloor may represent a significant fraction of Earth's total biomass.
Deep-sea sediments contain up to ten billion microbial cells per milliliter, according to research summarized by the Smithsonian Ocean portal.
Surface seawater, by comparison, typically contains around one million cells per milliliter.
These microbes metabolize a wide range of chemicals, including methane, sulfur compounds, iron, and manganese.
Some live in sediments hundreds of meters below the seafloor, in conditions with minimal energy availability and generation times measured in centuries.
Most microbial diversity is known only from genetic sequences. Culturing deep-sea microbes in the lab is difficult because their growth requirements are poorly understood.
Environmental DNA surveys reveal that the majority of sequences do not match any organism in existing databases.
These unknown sequences represent entire branches of the tree of life with no described representatives.
The genetic distance between some of these lineages and their nearest known relatives is larger than the distance between humans and jellyfish.
Cold seeps are areas where methane and hydrogen sulfide seep from the seafloor at near-ambient temperatures.
Like hydrothermal vents, they support chemosynthetic ecosystems. Microbes oxidize methane and sulfide, and larger organisms host these microbes as symbionts.
Cold seeps occur on continental margins worldwide and can persist for thousands of years, far longer than hydrothermal vents, which are often ephemeral.
Seep communities include clams, mussels, and tube worms similar to those at vents, but also species unique to seeps, such as ice worms that live on methane hydrate deposits.
Methane hydrates are crystalline solids in which methane molecules are trapped within a lattice of water molecules.
They are stable under the high pressure and low temperature conditions of the deep seafloor.
Vast deposits exist on continental slopes. Disturbance of these deposits, whether by warming or by extraction, could release methane, a potent greenhouse gas.
The organisms living on and around methane hydrates are adapted to an environment that is both an energy source and a geological hazard.
The figures in this script trace to bodies that conduct or coordinate deep-sea research.
NOAA Ocean Exploration provides expedition data and educational summaries. Ocean Census is a current global effort to describe marine species.
MBARI operates ROVs and submersibles and publishes observations from thousands of dives.
The Smithsonian Ocean portal synthesizes peer-reviewed research. These sources are named because the script's claims depend on their work.
We do not know how most deep-sea animals reproduce, how long they live, or how they interact with each other outside the moments captured on camera.
We do not know the total number of species. We do not know how deep-sea ecosystems will respond to warming, acidification, or mining.
The deep ocean is not a finished inventory. It is a habitat we are still learning to observe.
What lives in the depths of the ocean is mostly a question we are still answering.
The organisms we have named are a small fraction of what is there. The rest is pressure, darkness, and the ongoing work of looking.
